cues.text:
For more than two thousand years,
philosophers have tried to answer one
question.
What does it take to be happy?
Their answers don't agree.

Each one goes a little deeper than the
last.
So let's go down, one step at a time.

layers.text: “It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly.”
layers.highlight: living wisely and well and justly

layers.text: Principal Doctrines V · tr. R. D. Hicks

cues.text: At the top is Epicurus.

In a garden in Athens, he taught his
friends that pleasure is the point of
life.
But not the pleasure you might think.
In his words:

it is impossible to live a pleasant life
without living wisely and well and justly,

and it is impossible to live wisely and
well and justly without living pleasantly.

For Epicurus, a good life and a happy life
were the same life.

layers.text: Rembrandt, Aristotle with a Bust of Homer, 1653
“…it is not one swallow or one fine day that makes a spring, so it is not one day or a short time that makes a man blessed and happy.”
layers.highlight: it is not one day or a short time

layers.text: Nicomachean Ethics, Book I · tr. D. P. Chase

cues.text: One step down is Aristotle.

For him, happiness isn't a feeling you
have.

It's something you do: living out what you
are best at, and doing it well.
And it takes time.

As he put it: it is not one swallow or one
fine day that makes a spring,

so it is not one day or a short time that
makes a man blessed and happy.

layers.text: “Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.”
layers.highlight: the views which they take of things

layers.text: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 · tr. T. W. Higginson

cues.text: Deeper still are the Stoics.

Epictetus was born a slave, so he knew how
little of life we control.

He moved happiness to the one place no one
else can reach: our own judgements.

Men are disturbed not by things, but by
the views which they take of things.

Change the view, and the storm loses its
grip.

layers.text: “…life swings like a pendulum backwards and forwards between pain and ennui.”
Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Idea, § 57 · tr. Haldane and Kemp

cues.text: Then the ground gives way.

In 1818, Arthur Schopenhauer argued that
all wanting comes from lack,
and lack is a kind of pain.
Get what you want, and boredom moves in.
In his words,

life swings like a pendulum backwards and
forwards between pain and ennui.

On this view, lasting happiness was never
on offer.

layers.text: John Constable, Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds, c. 1825
“Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so.”

cues.text: At the bottom is a surprise.
In the autumn of 1826,

a young John Stuart Mill fell into a
crisis he could not shake.

What he took from it is the strangest
advice on this list.

Ask yourself whether you are happy, and
you cease to be so.

Happiness, he decided, comes by the way,
while you are aiming at something else.

Five steps down, the answers have turned
upside down.

Pleasure, then purpose, then control, then
doubt.
And finally: stop looking straight at it.
Maybe happiness isn't something you hold.

Maybe it's what happens while you're
holding something else.
